14 2023-03-12 02:00:00
15 2024-03-10 02:00:00


The series is mostly regular, but there are 15 times for which there’s no observation. We can use tsibble’s fill_gaps function to insert observations at these times (with missing values for the features):

hood = fill_gaps(hood)







Tip



Another way to check regularity is to compute differences between observation times with R’s built in diff function. In a regular series, the differences will all be equal.
Another way to insert missing observations is to use seq to create a regular sequence of times, then use merge or dplyr’s left_join to left join the sequence with the time series.


Finally, let’s check for missing values in the time series:

summary(hood)

      time                         temp_f      
 Min.   :2010-01-01 00:00:00   Min.   : 32.00  
 1st Qu.:2013-10-01 17:45:00   1st Qu.: 53.00  
 Median :2017-07-02 11:30:00   Median : 61.30  
 Mean   :2017-07-02 11:30:00   Mean   : 61.21  
 3rd Qu.:2021-04-02 05:15:00   3rd Qu.: 69.70  
 Max.   :2024-12-31 23:00:00   Max.   :102.10  
                               NA's   :696     


There are 696 missing values (39 of which we created) out of 131496 observations. Let’s create a new column to mark the observations where temperature is missing:

hood$na_temp = is.na(hood$temp_f)

Since temperature is only missing for a small proportion of observations, let’s impute the missing values. There are many different ways to do this. For instance, we can propagate prior non-missing values forward, aggregate the nearest non-missing values, or fit a model to the non-missing values and use its predictions.
The forecast package’s na.interp function can impute missing values in a vector or time series by linear interpolation:

library("forecast")

hood$temp_f = as.numeric(na.interp(hood$temp_f, linear = TRUE))

The argument linear = TRUE makes the function use linear interpolation; it can also impute values by time series decomposition (more about this in Section 11.3). The function returns a ts object, so we also need to convert it back to a vector with as.numeric.
Now that we’ve imputed the missing values, we can plot the series one more time with the imputed values marked. This is one way to check for patterns in (the former) missing values:

ggplot(hood) +
  aes(x = time, y = temp_f) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(data = filter(hood, na_temp), color = "red", size = 0.1)







Figure 11.3: Line plot of time versus temperature for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset, with imputed values marked in red.





Based on Figure 11.3, the former missing values are relatively spread out across the series. There appear to be a few clusters of missing values, which could indicate a multi-hour sensor failure. We’ll proceed with the imputed values. In practice, we should carry out further investigation of the missing values to look for patterns, identify potential causes, and evaluate how they might influence subsequent analyses. However, since the number of missing values was small, and this series includes a large number of observations, they’re unlikely to have much impact.

title: 11  Time Series
text:
11.3 Decomposition
Many time series can be decomposed into meaningful components:

A trend component: a smooth curve that follows long-term increases and decreases in the series. Some time series also exhibit long-term cycles: patterns of increases and decreases over irregular lengths of time. When a series has cycles, we call this a trend-cycle component.
One or more seasonal components: a curve which follows increases and decreases that repeat over a fixed (or regular) length of time. We call the fixed length of time a seasonal period or simply a season. There can be multiple seasonal components with different season lengths—we’ll see an example of this shortly.
A remainder component: the variation in the observations that’s left over after removing the trend and seasonal components. Generally, we want this component to be devoid of any trends, cycles, or seasonal patterns.

There are many different methods for decomposing time series.

11.3.1 Seasonality Plots
As a first step towards decomposition, let’s make a seasonality plot. In a seasonality plot, we split the time series into subseries by season, align each subseries to the same starting time, and then make a time versus feature plot with a separate line for each subseries. The idea is that any seasonal patterns will be visible in the plot as similarities between in the subseries.
The ggtime package provides functions to make seasonality plots for tsibbles. It also provides functions for other kinds of time series visualizations. The package is relatively new as of writing, so there are some missing features and bugs.
The ggtime function to make a seasonality plot is gg_season. The function requires three arguments: a tsibble, the name of the feature to plot on the y-axis, and the seasonal period. See ?gg_season for details about how to set the seasonal period; stricly speaking, this argument is optional, but it’s usually best to specify it.
Let’s make a seasonality plot where the seasonal period is one year for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series:

library("ggtime")

gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1y")







Figure 11.4: Seasonality plot with a 1-year seasonal period for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





There’s a clear pattern visible in Figure 11.4. At the beginning of the year, in Winter, temperatures are relatively low (about 50°F). They gradually increase over time until the peak in Summer (about 70°F). Then they gradually decrease as Winter approaches again. So this series has strong seasonality at the 1-year level; any decomposition we make should include a 1-year seasonal component.
It’s up to us to determine appropriate seasonal period(s) for a time series (although some functions will try to guess). In general, we should check the seasonality plots for any seasonal periods that we suspect might exhibit a pattern, regardless of whether that’s because we have expert knowledege about the processes that affect the series or because we see signs of the pattern in the initial time versus feature plots.
Let’s check the 1-month and 1-week seasonality plots:

gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1m")







Figure 11.5: Seasonality plot with a 1-month seasonal period for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





In Figure 11.5, it’s much harder to see a clear pattern than it was in Figure 11.4. One notable pattern is that there are small bumps over the course of the entire month; these suggest there might be seasonality over a shorter seasonal period.

gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1w")







Figure 11.6: Seasonality plot with a 1-week seasonal period for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





Figure 11.6 doesn’t exhibit any strong week-level patterns, but once again there are small bumps. They appear to correspond to days (there are seven bumps), so let’s check the 1-day seasonality plot:

gg_season(hood, temp_f, "1d")







Figure 11.7: Seasonality plot with a 1-day seasonal period for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





The annual seasonality we saw in Figure 11.4 makes it quite difficult to see patterns in the 1-day seasonality plot in Figure 11.7. The 1-day seasonality was easier to see in Figure 11.6. Based on what we know about earth, it seems likely that temperatures increase during the day and decrease at night.
After reviewing the seasonality plots for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series, we can conclude that there are seasonal effects at the 1-year and 1-day level. When we decompose the series, we should compute seasonal components at both of these levels.






Tip



The ggtime package’s autoplot function is a convenient way to make a time versus feature plot for a tsibble:

autoplot(hood, temp_f)








This is the same as Figure 11.2, but the code is much more concise. The autoplot function returns an ordinary ggplot2 object, so we can still add layers to customize the plot.




11.3.2 STL Decomposition
The Seasonal-Trend Decomposition Procedure Based on LOESS (Cleveland et al. 1990), commonly known as STL, is a very effective method for decomposing time series. An STL decomposition provides numerical estimates of the trend and seasonal components for a series.
The core of STL is a 2-step process:

Fit a seasonal component after removing the trend component.
Fit a trend component after removing the seasonal component.

These steps are repeated many times, starting from an initial trend component of 0 (no trend). STL uses LOESS (“locally estimated scatterplot smoothing”), a kind of local polynomial regression, to fit each component. Local polynomial regression approximates a smooth curve by fitting a polynomial (via least squares) at each point where the curve is to be evaluated. STL also uses some additional steps to handle spikes in series robustly; see Cleveland et al. (1990) for details.
In R, the feasts package provides an implementation of STL that works with tsibbles. To fit an STL decomposition, we can use the package’s model function, which is a generic interface for fitting models. The first argument must be the time series to decompose. The second argument must be a model description.
For an STL decomposition, we can use the STL function to write the model description. The function’s only required argument is a model formula, written with ~, which describes the decomposition. The left-hand side should be the feature to decompose. On the right-hand side, we can use the trend and season functions to describe which components to extract.






Tip



An STL decomposition always includes a trend component, so we can omit the trend function in the model description unless we want to set parameters related to the trend.
See ?STL for more details.


As a demonstration, let’s apply STL decomposition to the Sacramento River Water Temperature series. We’ll extract seasonal components at the 1-year and 1-day level, since we saw patterns there in Section 11.3.1. The code to fit the STL decomposition is:

library("feasts")

Loading required package: fabletools

stl_fit = model(
  hood,
  STL(
    temp_f ~ season("1y") + season("1d"),
    robust = TRUE  # make fit robust against outliers
  )
)

After fitting an STL decomposition, we’ll generally want to inspect or use the individual components. We can get the components as a tsibble with the components function:

stl_cmp = components(stl_fit)
stl_cmp

# A dable: 131,496 x 8 [1h] <UTC>
# Key:     .model [1]
# :        temp_f = trend + season_1y + season_1d + remainder
   .model         time                temp_f trend season_1d season_1y remainder
   <chr>          <dttm>               <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
 1 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 00:00:00   47.4  60.4   -0.172      -13.6     0.712
 2 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 01:00:00   47.6  60.4   -0.176      -13.6     0.916
 3 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 02:00:00   47.5  60.4   -0.109      -13.6     0.783
 4 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 03:00:00   47.6  60.4   -0.0554     -13.6     0.831
 5 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 04:00:00   47.7  60.4   -0.0138     -13.6     0.880
 6 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 05:00:00   47.7  60.4    0.0141     -13.6     0.891
 7 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 06:00:00   47.7  60.4    0.0112     -13.6     0.903
 8 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 07:00:00   47.7  60.4    0.0107     -13.6     0.888
 9 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 08:00:00   47.7  60.4   -0.0162     -13.6     0.918
10 "STL(temp_f ~… 2010-01-01 09:00:00   47.7  60.4   -0.0300     -13.6     0.915
# ℹ 131,486 more rows
# ℹ 1 more variable: season_adjust <dbl>


The result includes columns for the original series, the trend component (trend), each seasonal component (season_*), and the remainder (remainder) after removing the trend and seasonal components from the series. It also includes a column for the seasonally adjusted series (season_adjust), which is the series with only the seasonal components removed. The seasonally adjusted series is useful when we’re only interested in trend or want to use a forecasting method that assumes no seasonality.
The best way to inspect an STL decomposition is by plotting it. The ggtime package’s autoplot function automatically makes a per-component plot for STL components:

autoplot(stl_cmp)







Figure 11.8: STL components plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





From top to bottom, Figure 11.8 shows the original series, the trend component, the seasonal components, and the remainder. At the left-hand side of each panel, a gray bar shows the relative scale of the component: each gray bar has the same height in the units of the original time series.
The STL decomposition for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series shows a mostly flat trend (compare the heights of the gray bars in the panel for the original series and the trend component). The 1-year seasonal component has a parabolic shape, similar to the pattern in Figure 11.4.
By default, STL allows seasonal components to change slowly from one season to the next. Figure 11.8 suggests that this has caused some of the 1-year seasonal component to leak into the 1-day seasonal component—notice how the peaks in the 1-year and 1-day seasonal components are similar. The 1-day seasonal component also appears as a filled area instead of a curve because it fluctuates over hours, but the plot is on the scale of years. We can plot the 1-day component separately over a shorter time interval, say the first week of January 2024, to make patterns easier to see:

library("lubridate")
# Limit from 2024-01-01 to 2024-01-07.
lims = make_datetime(year = 2024, month = 1, day = c(1, 7))

autoplot(stl_cmp, season_1d) +
  xlim(lims)







Figure 11.9: 1-day seasonal STL component plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset, limited to the first week of January 2024.





Figure 11.9 reveals the pattern for each day and also shows how it’s slowly changing.






Warning



The ggplot2 package sometimes converts datetimes into dates, which can make hourly plots like Figure 11.9 visually misleading.
One way to ensure that a plot uses datetimes is to explicitly set the limits in terms of datetimes (not dates!), as we did for the figure.


For series where there are multiple seasonal components and the largest one leaks into the others, it can be useful to disallow gradual change for the smaller seasonal components. To do so, we refit the STL model with the setting window = "periodic" for the seasonal components where we want to disallow change:

stl_fit = model(
  hood,
  STL(
    temp_f ~ season("1y") + season("1d", window = "periodic"),
    robust = TRUE  # make fit robust against outliers
  )
)

stl_cmp = components(stl_fit)

autoplot(stl_cmp)







Figure 11.10: STL components plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset, with periodic 1-day seasonal component.





In Figure 11.10, the trend and 1-year seasonal components look about the same as with the previous model. The 1-day seasonal component looks like a black rectangle, again because it fluctuates over hours and the plot is on the scale of years. We can see the 1-day seasonal component better by focusing on a single week:

autoplot(stl_cmp, season_1d) +
  xlim(lims)







Figure 11.11: Periodic 1-day seasonal STL component plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset, limited to the first week of January 2024.





Figure 11.11 shows that starting from midnight each day, temperatures decrease until about 6 am, then increase until about 6 pm, then decrease again. The overall change in temperature is relatively small (less than 1°F).






NoteNote: STL Parameters



There are several parameters that can be adjusted in the STL decomposition. The automatic decomposition we used here is not necessarily the best one.
To learn more about these parameters, see ?STL and Cleveland et al. (1990).








NoteNote: Multiplicative Decompositions



Throughout this section, we’ve assumed that decompositions are additive: adding up the trend, seasonal, and remainder components gives the original series.
For a positive time series where the variations increase and decrease with the level of the series, it often makes more sense to use a multiplicative decomposition. In this case, multiplying the components gives the original series.
One way to achieve a multiplicative decomposition is to take logarithms of the series before decomposition. There are also decomposition methods that are specifically multiplicative (or have both additive and multiplicative versions).








NoteSee Also



There are several other methods for decomposing time series, ranging from simple to extremely complicated. Time series decomposition is often of interest to government agencies, so many of the methods have been developed by statisticians working for the United States and other countries. To learn more about these, see the Time Series Decomposition chapter of Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021).

title: 11  Time Series
text:
11.4 Autocorrelations
One more statistic we can use (and visualize) to investigate a series is autocorrelation. Autocorrelation is the correlation (Section 5.2) between a time series and a time-lagged version of the same time series. For instance, lag-1 autocorrelation is the correlation between the series and the series lagged (shifted back) by 1 time step. As correlations, autocorrelations are bounded between -1 and 1, with 0 indicating no relationship and -1 or 1 indicating a strong negative or positive relationship.
In practical terms, large lag-1 autocorrelation means that we can effectively predict an observation with the previous observation. Large lag-2 autocorrelation means there’s useful predictive information 2 observations back, and so on.
The ACF function in the feasts package computes autocorrelations for a tsibble. The first two arguments are the time series and feature, respectively. We can optionally set the lag_max parameter to specify how many autocorrelations to compute.
Let’s compute autocorrelations for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series:

hood_acf = ACF(hood, temp_f, lag_max = 24*5)
head(hood_acf)

# A tsibble: 6 x 2 [1h]
       lag   acf
  <cf_lag> <dbl>
1       1h 0.999
2       2h 0.999
3       3h 0.998
4       4h 0.998
5       5h 0.998
6       6h 0.997


We can use the autoplot function to make an autocorrelation plot, which shows lags on the x-axis and autocorrelations on the y-axis:

autoplot(hood_acf)







Figure 11.12: Autocorrelation plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





The autocorrelation plot shows two dashed horizontal lines at the upper and lower bounds for a significance test of zero autocorrelation. The test can be helpful for identifying which autocorrelations are likely to be zero. However, for a time series with a large number of observations, the bounds will be very close to zero, so even negligible autocorrelations will be considered statistically discernible. Thus it’s important to consider the actual autocorrelation value (the effect size) in addition to discernibility.






Tip



When a time series has a trend, the autocorrelations tend to be large at low lags and decrease slowly as the number of lags increases.
When a time series has seasonality, the largest autocorrelations tend to be at lags that are multiples of the seasonal period.


The autocorrelations for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series exhibit both patterns simultaneously, although Figure 11.12 only shows the trend pattern (try increasing the number of lags to see the seasonality pattern; remember that a year has approximately \(24 \times 365.25\) hours).

11.4.1 Partial Autocorrelations
Autocorrelations alone don’t give us a complete picture of the correlation structure in time series.
To understand the problem, consider a series with just three observations: \(y_1, y_2, y_3\). If the lag-1 autocorrelation is large, then \(y_1\) is correlated with \(y_2\), and \(y_2\) is correlated with \(y_3\). When we examine the lag-2 autocorrelation, the correlation between \(y_1\) and \(y_3\), the observations might be correlated on their own, or they might be correlated because both are correlated with \(y_2\). In other words, lag-1 autocorrelation affects lag-2 autocorrelation, and for longer series, this problem applies to all autocorrelations.
To overcome the problem, we also examine partial autocorrelation, which is the autocorrelation after removing the effects of observations at intermediary lags.
In R, the PACF function in the feasts package computes partial autocorrelations for a tsibble. The syntax is the same as for the ACF function.
The partial autocorrelations for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series are:

hood_pacf = PACF(hood, temp_f, lag_max = 24*5)
head(hood_pacf)

# A tsibble: 6 x 2 [1h]
       lag   pacf
  <cf_lag>  <dbl>
1       1h 0.999 
2       2h 0.167 
3       3h 0.0310
4       4h 0.125 
5       5h 0.0323
6       6h 0.0136


Once again we can use the autoplot function to make a partial autocorelation plot, which shows lags on the x-axis and partial autocorrelations on the y-axis:

autoplot(hood_pacf)







Figure 11.13: Partial autocorrelation plot for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





When a time series has seasonality, the partial autocorrelation tends to spike at the lag approximately equal to the seasonal period. Using partial autocorrelations to detect trend is difficult; use a plot of the series, a decomposition, or autocorrelations instead.
Figure 11.13 shows large partial autocorrelations at lag-1 and perhaps lag-2. All of the others shown are below 0.1.

title: 11  Time Series
text:
11.5 Stationary Series
A time series is stationary if the distribution at each time step doesn’t depend on the time. A series with trend or seasonality is never stationary. For instance, the Sacramento River Water Temperature series is clearly not stationary based on Figure 11.2 and Figure 11.10.
Visually, a stationary series displays no trend or seasonality, and the variance is constant (the fluctuations do not become noticeably smaller or larger over some time intervals). The [ARIMA Models][fpp-arima] chapter of Forecasting: Principles and Practices, 3rd edition (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021) provides several plots of stationary and non-stationary time series.
For a stationary series, the autocorrelations either decrease to zero rapidly or are all close to zero. Because of this, we’ll often use autocorrelation plots to help us assess whether a series is stationary.






NoteNote: Portmanteau Tests



There are several hypothesis tests designed to test whether the autocorrelations for a series are (mostly) zero, as we’d expect of a stationary series. These are collectively known as portmanteau tests because they test many autocorrelations at once. The Ljung-Box test is one of the most widely-used portmanteau tests.
These tests tend to be highly sensitive to sample size, and will almost always reject (which indicates the series is non-stationary) for time series with many observations.


When we fit a forecasting model (Section 11.6), as a diagnostic we can check that the residuals (for predictions of the training data) are stationary. If they’re not, then the model fails to capture some of the patterns in the series and a better model may exist.
Some forecasting models (such as ARIMA; see Section 11.6) assume the time series being forecasted is stationary. There are a few things we can do to transform a non-stationary series into a stationary series.
If the variance is not constant, taking the logarithm or a power of the series will often stabilize it.






Note



Logarithm and powe transformations are sometimes called Box-Cox transformations because they can be written in a more general form. There are automated methods to choose the best Box-Cox transformation for a series, although it’s still prudent to manually inspect the transformed series.


If a series has trend or seasonality, we have several options for forecasting. One approach is to decompose the series to remove the trend and seasonality, check that the remainder is stationary, and then forecast on the remainder. The remainder forecast can be combined with the trend and seasonal components to get a forecast for the series.
Let’s examine the remainder from the STL decomposition in Section 11.3.2 to check for stationarity. First, we’ll make a time versus feature plot. Figure 11.10 showed a few extreme values; we’ll remove those to make patterns easier to see:

autoplot(stl_cmp, remainder) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_minor_breaks = "1 year") +
  ylim(-10, 10)  #







Figure 11.14: Line plot of time versus temperature for the remainder component from the STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature series, with extreme values (below -10 or above 10) removed.





The remainder series appears to have (mostly) constant variance and no trend in Figure 11.14. Even with the extreme values removed, it’s difficult to tell from the figure whether there’s any seasonality.
Now let’s check the autocorrelation plot:

autoplot(ACF(stl_cmp, remainder, lag_max = 24*5))







Figure 11.15: Autocorrelation plot for the remainder component from the STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





Figure 11.15 shows large autocorrelations at all of the lags in the plot. The remainder series is clearly not stationary. If we want to use it for forecasting, we’ll need to choose a method that doesn’t require a stationary series.
Another approach to forecasting a non-stationary series is to take differences. In particular, take the series and subtract (or divide by) a lagged copy of the series. Differencing at lag-1 works well for many series, although if we have more context about the series, we may want to use a different lag. For instance, differencing at lag equal to the seasonal period can help remove seasonality. Occasionally, we might need to difference a series several times to get something stationary. After taking differences, we can check for stationarity, and then forecast on the differences.
Let’s try taking differences of the remainder series from the STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature series. We can use the tsibble package’s difference function to do so:

autoplot(ACF(stl_cmp, difference(remainder, 1), lag_max = 24*5))







Figure 11.16: Autocorrelation plot for the first differences of the remainder component from the STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





The autocorrelations for the differenced remainder series (Figure 11.16) are much smaller than the autocorrelations for the original remainder series (Figure 11.15). Almost all of the autocorrelations except the lag-1 and lag-3 are smaller than 0.05. The largest, at lag-1, is only about -0.2. Although the differenced remainder series isn’t a perfect example of a stationary series, it might be okay to use it with a forecasting model that requires stationarity. If we do, we can check that the residuals are approximately stationary; this is a more important diagnostic.

title: 11  Time Series
text:
11.6 Forecasting
As with decomposition, there are many different methods for forecasting or predicting future values of a time series. This section introduces just a few of the most well-known methods.
There are also many different R packages for forecasting, as we hinted at in Section 11.1. See that section for links to comprehensive guides. In this section, we’ll mostly use the fable package to fit forecasting models. Like the feasts package (from Section 11.3.2), the fable package uses the generic model function to fit models. The package also uses the generic forecast function to generate forecasts from fitted models.
Forecasting models tend to be computationally demanding. Forecasting on a time series with a large number of observations sometimes requires a lot of time and memory. To ensure that the examples in this section will run on the average laptop, we’ll subset the Sacramento River Water Temperature series down to just the final two years (2023-2024). Instead of filtering the dataset directly, we’ll use the components tsibble from the STL decomposition (Section 11.3.2), since that contains the original data as well as the components, which we might use later:

hood23 = filter(stl_cmp, year(time) >= 2023)

# Remove the `.model` column, since it causes problems for downstream modeling:
hood23 = select(hood23, -.model)

head(hood23)

# A tsibble: 6 x 7 [1h] <UTC>
  time                temp_f trend season_1d season_1y remainder season_adjust
  <dttm>               <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>         <dbl>
1 2023-01-01 00:00:00   50.9  60.1    0.0166     -12.6      3.44          63.5
2 2023-01-01 01:00:00   50.9  60.1   -0.0203     -12.7      3.55          63.6
3 2023-01-01 02:00:00   51    60.1   -0.0547     -12.7      3.69          63.8
4 2023-01-01 03:00:00   51    60.1   -0.0893     -12.7      3.69          63.8
5 2023-01-01 04:00:00   51    60.1   -0.125      -12.7      3.72          63.8
6 2023-01-01 05:00:00   51    60.1   -0.160      -12.7      3.73          63.8



11.6.1 Simple Methods
There are several relatively simple methods for forecasting:

Naive forecasting: use the most recent observation for all forecasts. In fable, this is the NAIVE model function.
Seasonal naive forecasting: use the corresponding observation from the previous seasonal period for each forecast. In fable, this is the SNAIVE model function.
Mean forecasting: use the mean of the series for all forecasts. In fable, this is the MEAN model function.
Drift forecasting: use the line that passes through the first and last observation for all forecasts. In fable, this is the DRIFT model function.

Let’s try forecasting for the Sacramento River Water Temperature series with the naive method. First, we fit the model with the model function:

library("fable")

naive_fit = model(hood23, naive = NAIVE(temp_f))

Next, we forecast with the forecast function (see ?forecast.mdl_df for help). Use the h parameter to set the number of forecasts. In this case, we’ll forecast the next 3 days:

naive_fcst = forecast(naive_fit, h = 24*3)

We can plot the forecasts with the autoplot function, adding an autolayer to also show the original series:

lims = tail(hood23$time, 1) + days(c(-29, 7))

autoplot(naive_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, temp_f) +
  xlim(lims)







Figure 11.17: 7-day naive forecasts for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





The forecasts (Figure 11.17) are automatically plotted with prediction intervals. Since we used the naive method, all of the forecasts are the same. The prediction intervals get wider at times farther into the future to indicate increasing uncertainty about the forecasts.






Tip



To extract the prediction intervals as numbers, use the hilo function. See ?forecast.mdl_df and ?hilo for more details.


As one more example, since this series exhibits strong seasonality, let’s forecast with the seasonal naive method. For this method, we must specify the length of the seasonal period with a model formula and the special lag function:

snaive_fit = model(hood23, snaive = SNAIVE(temp_f ~ lag("1y")))
snaive_fcst = forecast(snaive_fit, h = 24*3)

autoplot(snaive_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, temp_f) +
  xlim(lims)







Figure 11.18: 7-day seasonal naive forecasts for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset, where the seasonal period is 1 year.





The forecasts in Figure 11.18 vary over time since the seasonal naive method takes observations from the previous season as forecasts. This is also why the prediction intervals have constant width and are wider than in Figure 11.17; the forecasts are not necessarily better closer to the most recent observation.
Although the methods described in this section are simple, they often work surprisingly well. They’re also easy to interpret. For series with strong seasonal components, these methods can be improved without much additional complexity by decomposing the series, forecasting on the remainder series, and then recombining the forecasts with the seasonal components.


11.6.2 Linear Models
Linear models are especially useful for forecasting time series when there are meaningful predictors available, as is often the case for multivariate time series. Regardless of whether the time series is multivariate, linear models can be effective at modeling simple trends and relatively complex seasonality.
In fable, the model function for a linear model is TSLM. The function requires a model formula (just like the lm function). The model formula can include several special functions, such as:

trend to include a linear time trend.
season to include a categorical predictors for seasonality. The seasonal period must be specified. This creates one predictor for each time step (except the first) in the seasonal period, so it’s not recommended for long seasonal periods.
fourier to include Fourier predictors for seasonality. The seasonal period must be specified, and the number of predictors can optionally be specified. Fourier predictors are sine and cosine functions of time; just a few Fourier predictors can approximate most seasonal patterns well. Fourier predictors are appropriate to use even for long seasonal periods.

See ?common_xregs for a complete list of special functions.
Let’s fit a linear model to the Sacramento River Water Temperature series. We’ll include Fourier terms for 1-year and 1-day seasonality. Since linear models handle trend and seasonality reasonably well, we’ll forecast 1 year into the future:

tslm_fit = model(
  hood23,
  lm = TSLM(
    temp_f ~ trend() + fourier(24*365, 5) + fourier(24, 3)
  )
)

report(tslm_fit)

Figure 11.19: 1-year linear model forecasts for the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset, with Fourier terms for 1-year and 24-hour seasonality.





Figure 11.19 shows the forecasts and associated prediction intervals. For a linear model, the prediction intervals are estimated based on the variance of the residuals (this is true for any linear model, not just in the time series context).


11.6.3 ARIMA Models
An autoregressive integrated moving average model, or ARIMA model, is a combination of three simpler methods:

An autoregressive model, denoted AR(\(p\)) assumes each observation is a linear combination of the previous \(p\) observations and an error term.
The simplest AR model, denoted AR(1), uses only 1 previous observation. Mathematically, for an observation \(y_t\) and error term \(\epsilon_t\), the model is
\[
y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \epsilon_t
\]
The model estimates the values of the coefficients \(c\) and \(\phi_1\).
Integrated (I) refers to differencing, which is built into ARIMA models. The order of differencing is denoted by \(d\).
A moving average model, denoted MA(\(q\)) assumes each observation is a linear combination of the previous \(q\) error terms and a new error term.
The simplest MA model, denoted MA(1), uses only 1 previous error term. Mathematically, for an observation \(y_t\) and error term \(\epsilon_t\), the model is
\[
y_t = c + \theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1} + \epsilon_t
\]
The model estimates the values of the coefficients \(c\) and \(\theta_1\).

ARIMA models are denoted by ARIMA(\(p\), \(d\), \(q\)) to indicate the parameters for the three methods.






Warning



AR, MA, and ARIMA models all assume a stationary time series.
They will not necessarily work well for a series that isn’t stationary, and the estimated standard errors and prediction intervals will not be correct.
There is an extension of ARIMA for time series with seasonality (but not trend). The ARIMA model function (explained and demonstrated below) will automatically consider seasonal ARIMA models.


In fable, the model function for an ARIMA model is ARIMA. The function requires one argument: a feature to model or a model formula. With a model formula, we use the special pdq function to manually set the parameters \(p\), \(d\), and \(q\). When these are not specified, fable will automatically try to find the best settings by fitting and comparing multiple models.
Let’s try fitting an ARIMA model to the almost-stationary remainder component from the STL decomposition (Section 11.3.2) of the Sacramento River Water Temperature series. We’ll let fable select the best model automatically:

arima_fit = model(hood23, arima = ARIMA(remainder))
report(arima_fit)

Series: remainder 
Model: ARIMA(1,0,4)(1,1,0)[24] 

Coefficients:
         ar1      ma1     ma2     ma3     ma4     sar1
      0.9894  -0.0177  0.0562  0.0373  0.0228  -0.4072
s.e.  0.0011   0.0077  0.0076  0.0073  0.0076   0.0070

sigma^2 estimated as 0.009309:  log likelihood=16108.18
AIC=-32202.37   AICc=-32202.36   BIC=-32147.97


In this case, the best model was an ARIMA(1, 0, 4) model with a seasonal ARIMA(1, 1, 0) model for a 24-hour seasonal period.
Let’s use the model to forecast 1 year into the future:

arima_fcst = forecast(arima_fit, h = 24*365)

autoplot(arima_fcst) +
  autolayer(hood23, remainder)







Figure 11.20: 1-year ARIMA forecasts for the remainder component from the STL decomposition of the Sacramento River Water Temperature dataset.





Judging from Figure 11.20, it seems like the ARIMA model doesn’t fit well. While the forecasts do fluctuate slightly, they don’t appear to be that much different from the naive method or the mean method, despite the much more complicated model. This may be due to the lack of stationarity in the remainder series.






Warning



For any model, examining the residuals is critical for determining how well the model fits and whether its assumptions are satisfied.
The resid function returns the residuals as a tsibble for an fable model.
The ggtime package’s gg_tsresiduals function makes diagnostic plots for a time series model. These include a time versus feature plot, autocorrelation plot, and histogram for the residuals.








Tip



When forecasting is the primary goal, estimates of forecast accuracy are usually the best way to compare models.
We can estimate forecast accuracy by partitioning the time series into a training series and a testing series. Use only the training series to fit models, then forecast on the testing series to evaluate the models. The simplest way to do this is to treat (approximately) the first 80% of the series as training and the remaining 20% as testing. There are other, more sophisticated ways to partition time series into training and testing series that address specific limitations of this simple approach.








NoteSee Also



There are many, many other kinds of decomposition and forecasting models!
The textbook Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd Edition (Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021) is a good starting point for learning about more models. It also explains the statistics and algorithm fable uses to compare different ARIMA models.

title: 12  Repeated Measures
text:
12.1 Partial Pooling
This chapter introduces hierarchical models, multi-part linear models which are a fundamental tool for modeling repeated measures data. Along the way, we explain a few of the ideas that underpin these models.
Datasets often contain features that we can use to group the observations. For instance, a dataset where the subjects are people might include features such as city of residence, educational attainment, and marriage status. If one of these features (or one of the subpopulations they characterize) is important to our analysis goals, we’ll likely use the feature to group the observations during analysis.
Repeated measures datasets present another case where there are features we can use to group observations. Because the measurements for each subject are repeated, we might want to group observations by subject (or by time of measurement).
In the Orange Tree Growth dataset (Section 10.3), each tree has a unique ID number. We can use this to plot the observations for each tree separately:
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(Orange) +
  aes(x = age, y = circumference) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Tree)







Figure 12.1: Per-tree scatterplots of age versus circumference for the Orange Tree Growth dataset.
If we want to compute a statistic on a dataset with groups, two strategies we might consider are:
The no pooling strategy has the obvious advantage that it reveals details about the groups that we would otherwise miss with the complete pooling strategy. On the other hand, the complete pooling strategy also has an advantage: even if the number observations in some groups is small, by pooling them we’ll likely have enough observations to get an accurate estimate.
As an extreme case, consider what happens if some of the groups have only one observation. The estimates for these groups will likely be poor, because they depend entirely on sampling of a single observations. As an even more extreme case, if some groups are empty (no observations), then we can’t compute an estimate at all.
We can use a third strategy, partial pooling, to improve on the other two. The idea is to compute the no pooling estimates (for groups with observations) and the complete pooling estimate, then take the a weighted average (or linear interpolation) of the two. The average is weighted with the sample size and precision (inverse variance) of each estimate, so that:
In other words, partial pooling shares information between groups, while still providing a separate estimate for each one. It also allows us to compute estimates for groups with only zero or one observation.
Partial pooling is useful when working with repeated measures datasets because sometimes a measurement might be missing. It also leads to more accurate estimates even when all of the observations are there.

title: 12  Repeated Measures
text:
Compute a separate estimate for each group. This is a no pooling strategy, because we never pool the groups.
Compute one estimate, ignoring the groups. This is a complete pooling strategy, because we combine—or pool—all of the groups.





For groups with many observations and high precision, the average will be close to the no pooling estimate;
For groups with few observations and low precision, the average will be close to the complete pooling estimate.

title: 12  Repeated Measures
text:
12.2 Hierarchical Models
We can reap the benefits of partial pooling in a linear modeling context by using a hierarchical model. Hierarchical models are also known as multilevel models and linear mixed effect models (LMMs). They’re called hierarchical models because partial pooling is equivalent to fitting a hierarchy of models: one at the dataset level and one or more at the group level.
As a brief demonstration of how to fit a hierarchical model, let’s fit models with no pooling, complete pooling, and partial pooling. We’ll use the Orange Tree Growth dataset, with circumference as the outcome and age as a predictor. When we group the observations, we’ll group by tree.
Let’s start with the complete pooling strategy. We’ll fit a single model, ignoring the groups entirely:

# Complete pooling:
fit_compl = lm(circumference ~ age, orange)
summary(fit_compl)


Call:
lm(formula = circumference ~ age, data = orange)

There’s only one intercept in this model, computed based on all of the observations.
Next, let’s try the no pooling strategy. For this, we’ll fit the model with a separate intercept for each tree. To do so, we can add -1 in the model formula to remove the pooled intercept:

fit_no = lm(circumference ~ age + Tree - 1, orange)

Finally, let’s try the partial pooling strategy. The [lme4][] package is one of several packages we can use to fit a hierarchical model in R. We’ll use its lmer function, which is a lot like the lm function. In the model formula, we’ll add the groups as (1 | Tree). This is lme4’s notation for partially pooled intercept (another name for this is a random effect):

# Partial pooling:
library("lme4")

Loading required package: Matrix

fit_part = lmer(circumference ~ age + (1 | Tree) - 1, orange)
summary(fit_part)

   Data: orange

age 0.110113   0.004845   22.73


The residual standard deviation for the partial pooling model is only slightly higher than it is for the no pooling model, and we get the benefits of partial pooling.
The example in this section only shows the simplest way to use a hierachical model. There are many other ways to use them, such as computing partially pooled slopes, that are useful for all kinds of grouped datasets.

title: Overview
text:
One 2-hour session

This workshop introduces a variety of statistical methods and models to account for missing or censored measurements in datasets. We’ll begin by reviewing different types of missingness and censorship. We’ll then discuss specific models and strategies for imputation and estimation, when they’re appropriate, and when they break down. Extra emphasis will be given to techniques for working with nondetect (left-censored) measurements.

title: 13  Missing Data
text:
13.1 Why Data Are Missing
We say that data are missing or incomplete when some measurements are deliberately left out or left unspecified in a dataset. Just a few examples of why data might be missing are:
When data are missing, we have less information to use in analyses, so our conclusions are always weaker than they would’ve been with complete data. Certain kinds of missing data also interfere with how well a sample represents the population from which it was drawn, leading to inaccurate or biased results from standard statistical methods.
This chapter introduces a few general-purpose ways to think about, summarize, identify patterns in, and statistically account for missing data. Most of the methods described in this chapter assume that we have no information about the values of the missing data; for cases where we there is partial information, see Chapter 14.
The reasons why data are missing are the key to determining how they’ll impact statistical methods.
As a demonstration of this idea, consider a study of sea lion growth where the researchers weigh each of the sea lions in the study. Suppose their scale occasionally malfunctions and displays “ERROR” instead of a weight, so some of the sea lion weights are missing. Assuming the scale malfunctions randomly and independently of which sea lion is being weighed, we have no reason to expect that the observed weights and the censored weights are distributed differently. If we simply ignore the missing weights and proceed with a statistical analysis, our conclusions might be limited by lack of data, but they will still accurately (up to sampling error) reflect the population of sea lions.
On the other hand, suppose that the researchers’ scale only malfunctions and displays “ERROR” for especially heavy sea lions. Then the observed weights will mostly be from light sea lions and the missing weights will mostly be from heavy sea lions. If we ignore the missing weights and proceed with a statistical analysis, we’ll likely underestimate the typical weight of a sea lion, and other analyses may also be inaccurate. The reasons why the weights are missing matter for subsequent statistical work.
Little and Rubin (2019) divide reasons for missingness into three categories based on how they affect subsequent analyses (from least to most severe):
Unfortunately, there’s no statistical procedure to determine whether data are MNAR. This is inherent in what MNAR means: the cause of missingness is unknown—it’s the values of the missing data themselves or something that isn’t measured in the dataset. To conclude whether data are MNAR, we need a thorough understanding of how the data were collected.
Even for datasets where we’re confident (or comfortable assuming) that data are MCAR or MAR, statistical methods can’t tell us which is the case with complete certainty. There are some statistical tests we can apply, but like all statistical tests, these are subject to error.

title: 13  Missing Data
text:
Data are missing completely at random (MCAR) when the probability of being missing is equal across all observations, regardless of the measured value and of other features. In the sea lions example, weights from the scale that occasionally malfunctions randomly and independently are MCAR.
For data MCAR, simple methods for handling missing data are generally safe to use and yield accurate results.
Data are missing at random (MAR) when the probability of being missing is equal across observations after grouping by (or controlling for) other features in the dataset. That is, missingness depends on other features, but they’re recorded in the dataset. In the sea lions example, the weights would be MAR if the scale malfunctions more for certain researchers, and the dataset indicates which researcher recorded each weight.
For data MAR, we must account for the cause when we handle the missing data. Simple methods may yield inaccurate or biased results.
Data are missing not at random (MNAR) when the probability of being missing is unequal across observations even after controlling for other features in the dataset. In other words, the missingness is due to unknown, external features or due to the measured values. In the sea lions example, weights from the scale that malfunctions more for heavy sea lions are MNAR. Older texts sometimes refer to MNAR as “not missing at random” (NMAR).
Censored data, which are the subject of Chapter 14, are an example of MNAR data where the probability of being missing is 100% for measured values in specific known intervals.









Warning



How many data are missing is another important detail to consider before, during, and after analysis. Even when a dataset is structurally large (hundreds of rows and columns, for instance), if most of the data are missing, the information content can still be low.
Regardless of why data are missing, extreme lack of data leads to low-quality estimates (where the error is mostly due to sampling variation rather than bias in MCAR and some MAR scenarios).

title: 13  Missing Data
text:
13.2 Missing Data in R
R provides built-in support for missing data through the special value NA. It also provides functions to detect missing data (such as is.na) and parameters to ignore missing data (na.rm for most statistical functions).
There are many packages that extend R’s missing data capabilities. These three packages provide functions to clean, explore, and visualize missing data:

The naniar package (see the online documentation
The VIM package (after installing, see ?VIM)
The tidyr package (see the online documentation)

The naniar and VIM packages provide roughly similar functionality. The tidyr package is specifically focused on cleaning data (and not just missing data).
Most standard statistical methods require complete data. In order to accomodate missing data, we have two options:

Discard the observations with missing data;
Use a statistical model (such as a linear model) to fill the missing data with estimates.

For the latter, we recommend the popular mice package (which has online documentation); Section 13.5 explains more about why we recommend this package. The associated ggmice package provides supplementary functions to make ggplot2 plots.
In this reader, we use naniar for exploration and mice for filling missing data.






NoteSee Also



The CRAN Task View: Missing Data page is a curated list of R’s most widely-used packages related to missing data.
The website R-miss-tastic describes missing data workflows and packages for R (and to a lesser extent, Python). It also lists learning materials such as lectures, books, and example datasets. It’s updated regularly.

title: 13  Missing Data
text:
13.4 Visualizing Missing Data
When we explore a dataset with missingness, the goal is generally to understand how missing data within each feature are distributed relative to other features. In other words, we want to identify patterns and relationships. This kind of exploration is often helpful for distinguishing between data MCAR and MAR (Section 13.1), although it can’t tell us whether the data are MNAR. Exploring the missing data can also help us identify other limitations and potential problems, such as lack of sufficient data.
The key to exploring missing data is to create a shadow dataset, where each feature is replaced with a binary or categorical shadow feature that indicates missingess. We can do this on a per-column basis with R’s built-in is.na function. After constructing the shadow dataset, we can use standard exploration methods for categorical data (such as those in Chapter 2) to explore missingess.
Visualizations are a great way to explore data even when the data are missing. We can use the naniar package to produce several useful visualizations of missingness; the package is convenient because most of its functions compute the shadow dataset for us automatically.
Let’s use the California least terns dataset to demonstrate some of the missing data visualizations naniar provides. First, the vis_miss function makes a plot that summarizes missingness for an entire data frame:

library("naniar")

vis_miss(terns)







Figure 13.1: At-a-glance plot of missingness in the California least terns dataset.





Rows are represented by horizontal lines with a segment for each column. The lines are stacked vertically, matching the layout of rows in the data frame. Gray segments indicate observed data, while black segments indicate missing data. This way we can see which columns have missing data, how much data are missing, and where missing data co-occur.
Figure 13.1 shows that most of the features in the dataset are complete. There’s a small proportion (about 2%) of missing observations in the bp_, fl_, and total_nests features. There are slightly more (about 30%) in the nonpred_ features. The most dramatic missingness (about 93%) is in the pred_ and total_ (excluding total_nests) features, with a high degree of co-occurrence across these features.
An upset plot is another way to visualize co-occurrence of missing values. Upset plots are general-purpose plots for visualizing set intersections, but the naniar package uses them specifically to visualize missingness.
We can make an upset plot with the gg_miss_upset function. The nsets parameter controls how many features are shown. The nintersects parameter controls how many co-occurrences (across collections of two or more features) are shown:

gg_miss_upset(terns, nsets = 20, nintersects = 15)







Figure 13.2: Upset plot of missingness in the California least terns dataset.





The small horizontal bar plot on the left shows the number of missing data for each feature. The large vertical bar plot on the right shows the number of missing data co-occuring across each collection of features. Each collection of features is indicated below the vertical bar plot; a black dot means the feature is included in the collection. The function automatically selects the feature collections with the most co-occurrences.
Figure 13.2 provides additional information about the co-occurrences in the pred_ and total_ features: there are 477 co-occurrences across only those features, and there are another 134 across those features as well as the nonpred_ features. There are lower numbers of co-occurrences across other collections of features.
Another way to look for missing data patterns is to group with a categorical feature and then examine missingness within each group. This is especially helpful for checking whether data are MAR according to a particular categorical feature. The naniar package provides the gg_miss_fct function to plot missing data by group. The first argument should be the dataset, and the second argument should be the feature to group by:

gg_miss_fct(terns, year)







Figure 13.3: Plot of missingness grouped by year for the California least terns dataset.





The plot shows the groups along the x-axis and each feature in the dataset along the y-axis. The proportion of missing values in each (group, feature) combination is represented by a shaded rectangle. In this case, lighter colors indicate more missing data.
Based on Figure 13.3, the pred_ and total_ features are entirely missing from 2007 onwards. For other features with missing data, most of them are before 2016 or 2017.
Scatter plots are enormously useful for investigating relationships between features. When the features have missing data, we can still make a scatter plot by simply discarding the observations where either feature is missing. This allows us to see relationships in the observed data, but can also be misleading because it makes it easy to forget about the missing data entirely. The naniar package’s geom_miss_point is an alternative to geom_point that makes a scatter plot with the missing data shown. The missing data are represented by jittered points that lie well outside the range of the observed data; they’re also color-coded. Let’s make a scatter plot of total_nests versus fl_min, with missing data shown:

library("ggplot2")

ggplot(terns) +
  aes(x = total_nests, y = fl_min) +
  geom_miss_point(shape = "o")







Figure 13.4: Scatter plot of total nests versus minimum fledglings for the California least terns dataset.





Figure 13.4 shows that for this pair of features, there are only a few missing values (about 5-20) relative to observed values (hundreds).
In this section we’ve highlighted some of the most useful plots the naniar package provides, but see the reference for a complete list. The package also provides functions for exploring without visualizing (for instance, by making tables) and for filling missing data.

title: 13  Missing Data
text:
13.5 Statistics with Missing Data
Most statistical methods assume that all data are observed. For example, it’s unclear how to compute a sample mean when data are missing. In order to use these methods, we must modify the dataset so that there aren’t any missing data. We can do this either by discarding observations with missing data or by filling in the missing data.
First, let’s consider two common ways to discard observations:

In complete-case analysis, we discard every observation with missing data in any feature. Then we proceed with analysis.
The main advantage of complete-case analysis is its simplicity: special statistical methods are not necessary. The main disadvantage is that it wastes information—the incomplete observations may contain a lot of observed data.
Complete-case analysis is safe when data are MCAR. When data are MAR or MNAR, complete-case analysis can bias results.
In available-case analysis, we discard incomplete observations separately for each method based on the features that are needed. This means that we may use a different number of observations in each estimate or model!
The main advantage of available-case analysis is that it uses data more efficiently than complete-case analysis. The main disadvantage is that comparing or combining results where the number of observations differs is challenging, and some statistics—such as correlation—depend on being able to do so.
Available-case analysis is safe when data are MCAR. When data are MAR or MNAR, available-case analysis can bias results.

Now we turn to ways to impute, or fill in, missing data. The fundamental idea is to use a statistical model fitted on the observed data to predict the missing data. The model can be simple, such as computing a sample mean, or something more complicated. We’ll consider just two of many options for imputing missing data:

Sample means: for each feature, replace missing data with the mean of the observed data.
This is a poor way to impute data. The main advantage is that it’s simple and leads to unbiased estimates of means for data MCAR. The main disadvantage is that it biases most other statistics, regardless of why data are missing. As a specific example, it artificially lowers variance in the dataset, which leads to standard error estimates that are too small. Avoid using this approach.
Linear models: for each feature, fit a linear model on the observed data with the feature as a response and other features as predictors. Replace missing data with predictions from the model.
The main advantage of imputing with linear models is that it leads to unbiased estimates of means (and the model coefficients) for data MAR, provided that the features which influence missingness are included in the models. The main disadvantage is that it biases most other statistics. For instance, it leads to correlation estimates that are too large and standard error estimates that are too small. This approach is better than using sample means, but still leaves a lot to be desired.

Before we learn about a better way to impute missing data, let’s try sample mean imputation on the California least terns dataset in order to demonstrate why it’s problematic. We’ll impute two features, total_nests and fl_min, which each have a relatively small proportion of missing data (see Figure 13.1).
Before we impute, let’s construct shadow features to help us mark the imputed data on a plot later:

terns$na_total_nests = is.na(terns$total_nests)
terns$na_fl_min = is.na(terns$fl_min)

Now we can replace the missing data in total_nests and fl_min with the respective means of the features:

imp_mean = terns

imp_mean$total_nests[terns$na_total_nests] =
  mean(terns$total_nests, na.rm = TRUE)
imp_mean$fl_min[terns$na_fl_min] =
  mean(terns$fl_min, na.rm = TRUE)

To see why sample mean imputation is often a poor choice, let’s make a scatter plot of total_nests versus fl_min. We’ll use the shadow features to color-code the imputed data and visually de-emphasize the observed data (via transparency):

ggplot(imp_mean) +
  aes(
    x = total_nests,
    y = fl_min,
    color = na_total_nests | na_fl_min,
    alpha = na_total_nests | na_fl_min
  ) +
  geom_point(shape = "o") +
  scale_alpha_discrete(range = c(0.4, 0.8)) +
  lims(x = c(0, 250), y = c(0, 250)) +
  labs(color = "Imputed", alpha = "Imputed")







Figure 13.5: Scatter plot of total nests versus minimum fledglings for the California least terns dataset, with missing data replaced by sample means.





In Figure 13.5, notice that all of the imputed data lie on a horizontal line at the mean of fl_min. It’s difficult to see, but the rightmost imputed point is actually several points, all with the same coordinates. Compared to the observed data, variation in the imputed data is much smaller. The imputed data also deviate from the fan-shaped pattern in the observed data. For these features, the proportions of missing data were low, so the effect of imputing on subsequent analyses will be small. However, for features with more missing data, it could be substantial and lead to incorrect results.
After discarding or imputing missing data, we can use standard statistical methods, such as linear models:

fit = lm(fl_min ~ total_nests, imp_mean)
summary(fit)

lm(formula = fl_min ~ total_nests, data = imp_mean)

13.5.1 Multiple Imputation
Complete-case analysis is simple, but wastes data and only works well when data are MCAR. Available-case analysis makes it difficult to combine statistics for multiple features (and is also limited to data MCAR). Imputation with sample means or predictions from linear models tend to bias subsequent analyses. We need a better way to handle missing data.
Donald Rubin gets to the root of the problem with all of the techniques we’ve seen so far:

Imputing one value for a missing datum cannot be correct in general, because we don’t know what value to impute with certainty (if we did, it wouldn’t be missing).

This insight led Rubin and others to develop multiple imputation. The central idea of multiple imputation is to impute by creating multiple copies of the original dataset, where the imputed values are different in each copy. We then conduct statistical analyses on each copy. When we’re finished, we combine the results from all of the copies using two formulas known as Rubin’s rules.






NoteNote: Single Imputation



Single imputation refers to imputation techniques that only produce one dataset, such as those described at the beginning of Section 13.5.


Within the multiple imputation procedure, we can use any model we want to impute values for each copy of the dataset. We’ll generally chose models that include some randomness, so that we can simulate the randomness when making predictions and thus get different imputed values for each copy. For instance, we can use a linear model where we combine the predictions with simulated or sampled residuals.
Multiple imputation generally leads to unbiased statistics for data MCAR and MAR. When data are MNAR, the results can still be biased.






NoteNote: Sensitivity Analysis



When we suspect data are MNAR, a common two-step approach is to:

Conduct an analysis as if the data are MAR (or MCAR).
Conduct a sensitivity analysis that examines hypothetical “what-if” scenarios for the missing data, measuring how (and how much) the results of the step 1 analysis change.

Qualify the results and conclusions from the step 1 analysis with the results from the sensitivity analysis.


Several R packages implement multiple imputation, but mice (which stands for “multiple imputation by chained equations”) is the most widely-used package. The package provides functions that automate most of the steps in multiple imputation.
The package’s mice function performs multiple imputation. The first argument must be the original dataset. The parameter m controls the number of copies. The parameter method controls which model is used to generate predictions (see ?mice for a complete list).
Let’s compute multiple imputations for the California least terns dataset. We’ll make just 3 copies of the dataset. We’ll use the norm method, which fits a different linear model on each copy and uses it to make a prediction with a randomly sampled residual:

library("mice")

imp = mice(terns, m = 3, method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)

The mice package’s complete function provides access to the copies of the dataset. Let’s make a scatter plot of total_nests versus fl_min for each copy, with the imputed data marked (similar to Figure 13.4):

ggplot(complete(imp, "long")) +
  aes(
    x = total_nests,
    y = fl_min,
    color = na_total_nests | na_fl_min,
    alpha = na_total_nests | na_fl_min
  ) +
  geom_point(shape = "o") +
  scale_alpha_discrete(range = c(0.4, 0.8)) +
  lims(x = c(0, 250), y = c(0, 250)) +
  labs(color = "Imputed", alpha = "Imputed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.imp))







Figure 13.6: Scatter plots of total nests versus minimum fledglings for the California least terns dataset, for each copy generated by multiple imputation. In each plot, imputed data are marked.





The mice package provides a modified version of R’s built-in with function to make conducting analyses on all copies of a multiply imputed dataset convenient. For instance, this code fits a linear model with outcome fl_min and predictor total_nests on each copy:

fits = with(imp, lm(fl_min ~ total_nests))

The package’s pool function uses Rubin’s rules to combine results from multiple copies of a multiply imputed dataset. This code computes the final estimates from the fitted linear models:

summary(pool(fits))

         term   estimate   std.error statistic       df      p.value
1 (Intercept) 11.1652227 2.784864846  4.009251 756.6614 6.694645e-05
2 total_nests  0.1806421 0.008308291 21.742394 785.6743 1.994992e-82


For these features, the results are almost the same as when we used sample mean imputation (Section 13.5). This is because the proportion of missing data is very low; we would see a more dramatic difference if the proportion was higher.






NoteSee Also



Statistical Analysis with Missing Data (Little and Rubin 2019) is a definitive textbook about missing data. The authors provide detailed explanations of most methods in use today (some of which they created).
Handbook of Missing Data Methodology (Molenberghs et al. 2014) is an anthology similar in scope and depth to Little and Rubin (2019). It’s an excellent companion or alternative to that book.
Flexible Imptuation of Missing Data (van Buuren 2021) was written by the creator of the mice package for R and provides some examples of how to use the package. The first chapter is an excellent, intuitive overview of missing data concepts and methods.
